#9754. It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Bot detection has become a losing game. Security teams need to limit privileged access for humans and their machine counterparts equally.

The Internet is flooded with bots. People use them to organize their emails, shop, chat, and handle some of their busywork.

At the other end of the spectrum sit attackers who want to increase their speed just as much as, if not more than, legitimate users. The faster they can conduct distributed denial-of-service attacks or brute-force password attacks, the quicker they can breach an organization and the more victims they can claim.

The line between legitimate and illegitimate activity grows finer by the minute, as bots have become pros at mirroring human behavior — even its flaws. For example, during the infamous incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, bots reportedly found ways to communicate with one another by accessing the outside Internet — something they weren't programmed to do.

Behavioral baselines that security teams once relied on are becoming moot, since bots can impersonate humans. As the volume of bots accelerates, the real question isn't human versus bot but what that activity is telling teams and how to police it.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Security tools will miss something, so teams should choose systems that allow them to quickly edit, adjust, and continually adapt to a changing environment, explains Jeremy London, director of engineering, AI, and threat analytics at Keeper Security.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents, which can perform automated actions similar to bots without human oversight, are only adding to environmental complexities. While some advancements can be exciting, they also introduce more gaps and zero-day vulnerabilities to the attack surface that "we just didn't understand," London says.

"I think the continual effort, as a security organization, is to show up with the right tooling, understand what you're trying to solve for, and then be able to react quickly because your control plane probably missed something — that's a guarantee," London tells Dark Reading.

Organizations underwent significant transformations over the past decade, propelled by AI. Adoption moved at a scale that "no one ever predicted," London says. That has forced teams to cut corners on important safeguards.

Code reviews and security practices need a serious makeover, especially regarding boundaries and compliance. Bots and agents have new levels of autonomy and access, leading to more unpredictability and changing what security risks even look like.

However, such a makeover has proved to be a difficult undertaking because AI doesn't come with a security playbook, London explains. A decade ago, bots were rigid and scripts performed a single action. Now "teams vibe code stuff and throw things at the wall and see what works, and the scale that [bots] can operate at is totally different," he says.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

While organizations struggle, attackers are having a field day with these advancements. Given all of the recent disclosures and reports, it's no surprise that attacks are rising. What is surprising is how quickly threat actors can adapt and respond to countermeasures, says Jérôme Segura, VP of threat research at DataDome, a bot management and agent trust platform.

"Anytime we put challenges in front of them, we see it slows them down and costs them more because to run the same operation, they have to use more resources, which becomes expensive," he explains.

The reason the attackers aren't giving up despite the obstacles is that their attacks are working, Segura tells Dark Reading.

"Because the payout is so great, they're doubling, tripling their investments," he says.

The persistence is challenging and frustrating for defenders. But it's just the stark reality that threat actors are highly motivated, and "we're battling against that," Segura adds.

When threat actors use bots against online retailers, they replicate the exact flow of a human but without all the telltale signs, such as hesitating over a purchasing decision, fumbling to enter card or shipping details, or pausing to solve a CAPTCHA challenge. They don't need to click through every page like a human would or wait for the site to load all the images either. As a result, bots complete transactions in a split second, Segura says. The speed can create security risks and unfair competition for legitimate users.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

More concerningly, bots complete these tasks in ways that appear legitimate because they're aware that companies are trying to block this malicious activity, he says. And the volume is only increasing. Segura conducted research analyzing traffic hitting retailers' product pages and found that 91% were actually bad bots.

Taking legal action is difficult when it's nearly impossible to differentiate legitimate and illegitimate activity, which puts even more pressure on businesses. Scraping product pages or ticket scalping remains "kind of a gray area in terms of the legal aspect," Segura explains, adding that the law isn't quite clear yet on what is permitted.

In some cases, the culprits are organized groups just looking to make money and oftentimes use loopholes to circumvent the law. For example, they end up using existing infrastructure to collect scarce products and resell them, Segura says.

Threat actors organize so that they have specialties, just as defenders do, he has observed. Some specialize in reverse engineering specific parts of a website's code to understand how it works. Others focus on providing the necessary infrastructure, including all the IP addresses, to carry out those kinds of attacks, he says.

"You can source IPs from real users that are extremely convincing because they're also shared by humans," Segura explains. "So all these specializations within these groups, working well together, and making sure everybody's getting paid, is really interesting."

Behavioral analytics are struggling right now, London says, and is a "pain point" rippling across the industry.

Some bots can move the mouse pointer and send keystrokes to mimic typing, so verification techniques like measuring mouse movements or typing speeds need to evolve. Models can be a bit slow, just as humans can be, he notes.

"Although they are robotic in nature, some of those behavioral or human factors that teams have been using for indication points are really close," London says.

Since it's so difficult to determine whether activity is from a human or a bot, organizations should manage them both the same way when it comes to privileged identity: the less access, the better.

Given all of the risks and potential blast radii, "security teams, not developers, should probably decide whether AI is allowed in an organization," London recommends.

"From a security perspective, it makes it somewhat simple because AI agents can do bad things [and] humans can do bad things," he says. "So if we just look at it through that perspective, I don't care if it's a human or an agent."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9753. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. #9752. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9751. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9750. Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

Researchers discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages as part of a fake recruitment campaign that spreads malware and gives attackers access to developers' machines.

A coordinated supply chain campaign is targeting .NET developers with fake coding assignments, weaponized software dependencies, and GitHub-hosted malware capable of stealing browser credentials and establishing remote access.

Researchers at Socket discovered the campaign, which involves 13 malicious NuGet packages designed to compromise Windows-based developer environments through seemingly legitimate job assessments, according to a report published this week. The packages use fake job "Home Assessment" projects to target Windows .NET developers, with most posing as button controls for WinUI 3 and WPF, which are user interface frameworks for building applications.

"In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable," Socket researcher Kush Pandya wrote in the report.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

As in similar campaigns that weaponize developer repositories and code packages, attackers are exploiting developers' willingness to download, build, and run code they believe to be trustworthy. In this case, the malicious code is disguised as part of job-recruitment exercises for .NET developers. Such campaigns can turn routine development activities into infection vectors, potentially spreading malware and malicious code through the software supply chain.

NuGet is a package manager for .NET. Socket researchers traced the campaign across NuGet, GitHub repositories, and malicious code embedded in development projects, identifying packages linked through shared attack infrastructure and techniques.

The most recent example they found was a GitHub repository created on Nov. 4 that contained a purported WinUI 3 assessment called "Mini File Vault & Tracker." The project instructed candidates to complete a three- to four-hour development exercise using a supplied Visual Studio project. However, its dependencies contained malicious code.

"Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026," Pandya wrote in the report.

Socket could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reached candidates, as researchers found "no recruiter message, email or job post for them," he added.

The attack involved two malicious NuGet packages working together. One executed code after every project build, while the other launched a staged executable when the application created its button control. This effectively turned an ordinary development workflow into an infection chain.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

The investigation eventually uncovered 13 unique package names and 28 versions across those packages, as well as four NuGet publisher accounts linked to the operation.

Characterizing the campaign as posing a very serious threat to enterprises, Pandya says attackers could gain access to a "treasure trove" of sensitive information by compromising a developer's machine.

"A developer's machine holds source code, SSH keys, GitHub, package registry and cloud tokens, and browser sessions that have often already passed multifactor authentication," Pandya tells Dark Reading. "In this campaign, building the take-home project was enough to run the threat actor's code."

Beyond access to terminals and configuration files, many developers who work from a console have their command history automatically collected, he says. This can give adversaries insight into the commands developers have executed, as well as access to passwords and API keys that may have been inadvertently pasted into the command line, he adds.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Moreover, by disguising their activity as legitimate development work, attackers gain a degree of stealth and control once the malicious code is running on a developer's machine, he says.

"A threat actor could extract SSH keys and network configurations, but their access is still from an external host and must go through various security controls," Pandya explains. "If they are working directly from a developer's machine, they not only have the necessary access keys but also the expected IP address and geolocation to avoid suspicion."

As adversaries continue to weaponize code packages from legitimate sources to compromise the software supply chain, developers and security teams must remain vigilant. Socket has recommendations for both.

Developers should treat take-home coding assignments and unfamiliar projects as untrusted code, Pandya advises. Before building them, they should check for unfamiliar NuGet dependencies, additional package sources, and build scripts that could execute automatically.

"Open take-home tests and unfamiliar repositories only in a disposable virtual machine with no credentials," he recommends. "Restrict which package sources projects can use, scan dependencies before they are installed, and verify recruiters through official channels."

Organizations should also restrict which NuGet feeds developers can use and review third-party packages that contain build scripts capable of executing commands, according to Socket. They should also educate employees and job candidates about fake recruitment assessments to reduce the risk of attackers exploiting the hiring process to gain access to developer environments.

Security teams, meanwhile, should identify affected developer machines and treat suspected infections as potential credential and software supply chain compromises, rather than simply malware incidents, Pandya says.

"If a machine is compromised, isolate and reimage it, rotate credentials and tokens from a clean device, revoke active sessions, and review audit logs," he says.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9749. Every Industry Gave AI Their Data

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Software has the highest AI trace density because code, commits, tickets and incidents record the decisions behind the work, not just the data, giving AI more to learn from.

Your engineers are excited about AI, but they're often talking about it very differently than the rest of the business. That gap is already familiar across most technology companies. Sales teams are experimenting with AI for research and summarization. Marketing teams use it to accelerate drafting and content production. Operations teams use it to automate routine workflows.

The gains are real, but they are often incremental.

Engineering teams see something much bigger. Inside many B2B software companies, AI is no longer just a productivity tool. Developers increasingly treat it as a fundamental shift in how software gets built. They trust it to explain code changes, investigate regressions, predict failures before deployment, and accelerate defect resolution.

The common explanation is that AI works better in engineering because models were trained on code, programming languages are precise, or developers pushed the tools harder first.

The real reason is that software accidentally gave AI something far more valuable than data: trace density, the ratio of recorded reasoning to recorded outcomes. And it explains why AI feels native in engineering first—and why agents are the first mechanism every other industry can use to build the same advantage deliberately.

Most enterprise systems are designed to preserve outcomes, not decisions or reasoning.

A CRM records the final deal value. A ticketing system marks an issue as “resolved.” A codebase reflects the current state of the system. But very few systems preserve the chain of reasoning that produced those outcomes in the first place.

Why was the discount approved? Why did the timeout change from 5 seconds to 30? Why was one architecture path rejected while another moved forward?

Those decisions mattered. The reasoning behind them shaped production behavior, customer outcomes, and operational risk. But in most organizations, that reasoning disappears almost immediately after the decision is made.

This is the two clocks problem, a concept that also sits at the center of context graphs and engineering world models. There is a state clock and an event clock. The state clock tells you what is true now. The event clock explains how it became true.

Most enterprise software is excellent at preserving the first and remarkably bad at preserving the second.

This is why so many AI initiatives disappoint once they move beyond phase 1.

Most systems can capture what changed, what failed, what was approved. Very few can show how decisions were actually made. They lose what evidence was available at the time, which constraints mattered, what tradeoffs were debated, which alternatives were rejected, and why the final decision won.

Outcome data tells AI what happened. Decision traces teach AI how judgment works inside an organization.

That distinction matters because decision traces are fundamentally different from operational traces like logs, metrics, or observability data.

One helps you reconstruct events; the other helps AI learn precedent, tradeoffs, and decision-making patterns.

Without that layer, connecting an LLM to systems of record usually produces shallow intelligence. It is like training a lawyer on verdicts without case law: they see the outcomes, but not the deliberations, the rejected arguments, the reasoning that shaped the decision. The model can retrieve information, summarize documents, and surface patterns. But it cannot reliably exercise judgment without the reasoning that shaped prior decisions.

That’s why trace density, not data volume, is the hidden variable behind AI capability. That ratio—recorded reasoning to recorded outcomes—is what separates AI that retrieves from AI that thinks. And software happens to be the most trace-dense domain modern AI has ever encountered.

Software accidentally built the richest reasoning archive in modern work.

Not because engineers documented more than everyone else, but because software workflows systematically captured decisions, tradeoffs, failures, feedback loops, and the reasoning behind them at a scale few other industries could match.

That is why AI feels unusually capable inside engineering teams today—whether it is generating code, explaining changes, investigating regressions, or predicting the impact of a deployment before it reaches production.

Most explanations focus on the surface layer: models trained on code, structured programming languages, or developers adopting AI tools earlier than everyone else.

Those factors helped, but they are downstream effects of something much deeper.

Engineering workflows evolved in a way that continuously preserved reasoning.

Long before anyone talked about “trace density,” software teams were already generating it by default. Three structural forces made that possible.

In most professions, seniority eventually replaces explanation. A senior lawyer does not need to document every tradeoff behind a decision. A senior executive rarely explains every rejected path. A seasoned oncologist’s records capture the patient’s history and symptoms, but the reasoning behind the diagnosis is shaped by years of training and clinical experience. Authority itself becomes the reasoning.

Engineering culture developed differently. Open source development shifted the standard for how decisions were justified. Contributors couldn’t simply rely on title, tenure, or organizational authority to push a change through. They had to explain why the change should exist, why one implementation was better than another, and what tradeoffs they were making.

Title mattered less. Explanation mattered more.

A random contributor needed enough context to evaluate the decision as clearly as the architect who designed the system. Over time, reasoning stopped living only inside people’s heads. It became embedded directly into commits, reviews, and discussions that anyone could revisit later.

The workflow itself started preserving precedent.

Most industries rely on delayed human feedback loops.

Managers, reviewers, and executives interpret outcomes after the fact. Feedback is filtered through hierarchy, incomplete information, memory, and politics. By the time it arrives, the original reasoning is often gone.

Engineering environments work differently. The compiler has no bias. The test suite doesn’t care who wrote the code. Production doesn’t give exceptions for confidence, seniority, or good intentions.

If the reasoning behind a change was flawed, the system breaks. And it usually breaks quickly. Weak reasoning turns into incidents, regressions, outages, and 2 a.m. pages that force teams to reconstruct exactly what happened and why.

That pressure made explanation unavoidable.

Engineers learned to document decisions, justify tradeoffs, and preserve reasoning because the operational cost of not doing so was immediate and painful. Over time, those explanations accumulated into institutional memory that other engineers could learn from later.

Software did not just create better individual decisions. It created reusable organizational reasoning.

Most professions preserve the clean conclusion. Software preserves the messy process.

Pull requests, commits, diffs, code reviews, incident investigations, rollbacks, and deployment discussions don’t just record what changed. They preserve what almost changed, which alternatives were rejected, and why one path ultimately won. The reasoning gets attached to the exact moment it was used—and that is rare in almost any other domain. Software is the exception, not the rule.

Over the last 30 years, engineering workflows quietly accumulated an enormous archive of recorded judgment, tradeoffs, failures, and corrective decisions. Modern AI inherited that archive before anyone fully understood what software workflows were actually producing. That's exactly why every other industry faces the same problem: they have outcomes, but no event clock. Agents are the first practical mechanism to build one.

Trace density doesn’t increase because an organization logs more events. It increases when agents own a meaningful share of decisions.

That’s the threshold where capability changes, because that’s where decision traces actually get created.

The operating model starts to invert. Where humans once owned workflows and agents assisted, agents begin orchestrating the work itself—with humans stepping in where judgment is needed.

Most companies today still use AI as an assistant layer. A user asks a question, the model returns an answer, and the workflow continues exactly as before. That creates outputs, but not trace density. Trace density starts compounding when agents move inside the execution loop itself—where decisions are actively being made.

An agent operating inside the workflow gathers context, evaluates options, proposes actions, routes approvals, observes outcomes, and continues adapting as the situation changes.

In other words, the agent starts holding the bag from problem creation to resolution.

And between each step, dozens of decisions are constantly being made:

As the agent moves through the workflow, it continuously reasons between actions to connect one step to the next.

That reasoning—the logic happening in the gaps between actions—is the raw material for decision traces. When that reasoning is captured, preserved, and made available for future analysis, it becomes a record of how work actually gets done.

This is where trace density starts to accumulate. Not from the actions themselves, but from preserving the decision-making process that connects one action to the next.

This is why placement matters more than prompting. An agent outside the workflow returns answers. An agent inside the workflow creates infrastructure.

A chatbot can summarize a support ticket. An embedded agent can investigate the issue, correlate telemetry, simulate likely failure paths, propose a fix, route approvals, observe the outcome, and preserve the reasoning behind every step. Its movement becomes the learning signal, and the output matters less than the path. Agents are not random walkers moving blindly through systems. They are informed walkers pushed forward by real operational problems, and every step leaves a decision trace. As they traverse tickets, code, telemetry, deployment history, user sessions, approvals, and production behavior, they begin exposing structural relationships that static systems of record never capture on their own.

The graph already exists, but most of its connections live inside people’s heads. The agent’s path through the work becomes the event clock the organization never had.

Over time, those repeated trajectories begin surfacing patterns that were previously invisible: which systems tend to fail together, which approval chains consistently correlate with risk, which deployment sequences repeatedly trigger regressions, and which escalation paths actually resolve incidents fastest.

That’s how trace density becomes a context graph. Not a graph of nouns. A graph of decisions with evidence, constraints, and outcomes.

Most observability systems investigate failures after they happen. They can show which deployment preceded an incident, where latency increased, or which dependency failed first.

But they usually cannot preserve the reasoning layer itself. Why one mitigation path was chosen over another, which incidents shaped the response, which risks were considered acceptable, and how the organization learned what “good judgment” looked like in practice. Decision traces change that.

When agents operate inside execution loops, every regression investigation, PR simulation, rollout decision, support escalation, and defect resolution leaves behind machine-readable precedent. The system can preserve operational reasoning, not just operational state. That’s the difference between observability and compounding intelligence.

Over time, those accumulated traces start forming something much more valuable than incident history: an engineering world model. Unlike a system that simply stores information about the environment, it learns the dynamics of how the environment behaves under change: which systems fail together, which deployment patterns create risk, and how production behavior evolves after specific actions are taken.

With enough accumulated trace density, the system can stop reasoning only from retrieval and start reasoning from learned organizational physics. At that point, the questions become fundamentally different: not only what broke, but what will break. Which customers are likely to be affected? Which failure paths are emerging right now? What action is most likely to succeed next?

A system that can answer “what if” is no longer functioning like search. It is simulating the operational environment itself. That’s where AI stops being merely helpful and starts becoming operationally trustworthy.

Every other industry can start building the same advantage deliberately. Not by collecting more documents, but by designing agents that preserve reasoning as they work.

Put agents where decisions actually happen. Require them to show their work. Capture what they observed, which constraints shaped the decision, what alternatives they considered, and why one path ultimately won. Treat every decision as future training data for the system itself.

Because the next AI moat is not data. Its decision trace density. The companies that win over the next decade won’t be the ones with the most information—they’ll be the ones whose systems continuously preserve operational judgment as work happens.

Software accidentally spent 30 years building the world’s richest archive of recorded reasoning before anyone understood how valuable it would become. Now every industry has the opportunity to build that same advantage intentionally.

The engineering world model is what that advantage looks like in practice. To see how PlayerZero builds trace density into engineering world models, explore Context Graphs: Building Engineering World Models for the Age of AI Agents.

#9748. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9747. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9746. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

The revelation that 28 separate residential proxy services were found exiting the White House network is incredibly alarming. It’s especially troubling given how easily these services can be rented for a few dollars, essentially creating public access to a highly confidential network. This situation clearly represents a significant national security risk that warrants urgent investigation.

#9745. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.
