#9744. For the Love of Code

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

AI hasn't killed the joy of coding, but it has moved the craft up the stack, and that's where the problem-solving now lives.

Does coding still feel joyful, or does it just feel like output? That question's become a real conversation among developers over the past year. It's not two people trading opinions, but a pattern showing up across YouTube and Reddit, from veterans a decade or more into their careers to developers just breaking in.

Alex Kondov, a software engineer, gave that feeling one of its sharpest articulations: after twelve years of programming, he described AI as having compressed the part of the job he loved most—sitting with a hard problem, reading documentation and GitHub issues, trying and discarding solutions until one finally fit. In its place, he found himself reviewing AI-generated answers and reasoning through their second- and third-order effects.

It’s the same loss many engineers are describing. They didn’t fall in love with software to supervise an AI that writes code for them. They loved the craft of it: weighing two or three ways to solve a problem and picking the one that actually fits, writing something clean enough that it's still readable a year later, tracing strange behavior through a system, testing a theory, and finally understanding why something worked.

AI-assisted coding has changed where that craft lives. But the joy isn't gone—it's relocated to a level most of the current conversation hasn't caught up to yet: the system, not the line of code.

The engineers who find their way back to it are figuring out where the interesting problems are and working on them there.

AI coding tools are making engineers dramatically faster at implementation. Features get scaffolded in minutes. Refactors that once took hours now happen almost instantly.

And yet, teams still feel overloaded. According to recent research by Atlassian, 68% of developers now save more than 10 hours a week using AI tools. Still, half of them lose 10 or more hours a week right back to digging for context they don't have: tracking down who owns a service, re-explaining an incident to the third person who's picked it up, chasing a config change through a system no one fully documented.

In other words, coding itself is no longer the primary bottleneck.

This isn't the first time the ground has shifted under engineers. Machine code gave way to assembly, then high-level languages. Next came frameworks, cloud infrastructure, and sophisticated tooling that steadily removed low-level implementation work from developers' workflows.

When higher-level languages became mainstream, some feared that developers would stop reasoning deeply about computers. When frameworks automated more of the stack, others argued that engineering would become little more than assembling prebuilt systems.

AI-assisted coding has triggered a similar reaction. If machines can generate implementation details, what meaningful work is left for engineers to actually do?

However, abstraction has never eliminated engineering value. Each shift simply changed where that value lived. Engineers became responsible for broader systems, larger tradeoffs, and more operational complexity. The craft evolved alongside the systems being built.

Traditional programming creates a tight feedback loop: engineers explore the system directly, test assumptions in real time, wrestle with implementation details until the architecture finally clicks into place. For a lot of engineers, that loop was where the satisfaction actually lived—writing something rough, debugging it, fixing it with something slightly less rough, and getting the hard-won rush of finally understanding a problem. Remove that struggle, and the work starts to feel a little more automatic and a little more lifeless.

What makes AI-assisted coding feel emotionally different is the workflow itself. More of the interaction shifts from exploring a problem firsthand to evaluating, steering, and refining generated solutions. The workflow is faster, but it creates more distance from the process of arriving at an answer.

Maximilian Schwarzmüller, a developer and instructor with 3 million students, reached a similar conclusion in a video pointedly titled, "It was more fun before AI." Fundamentals and understanding the code still matter, but as he puts it, "the writing code part is definitely going away." Not gone entirely, but a fundamentally different job than it was even a few years ago.

That emotional shift is real. It doesn't mean engineering skill is disappearing. But the abstraction is arriving faster than many teams can absorb.

AI-generated code increases output, but also increases the amount of software that engineers are responsible for maintaining, debugging, and operating in production.

More generated code means more dependencies, more interactions between services, more edge cases, more regressions, and more operational complexity distributed across systems.

That burden doesn't land evenly. Senior engineers become the team's unofficial system model, the people who know which services misbehave under load, which deployment patterns have caused regressions before, which customer environments behave differently, and why. None of that lives in a document. It builds up over years of being the one who got paged.

AI-generated systems move faster than documentation and coordination can keep up with, and that’s where today’s AI copilots fall short. Copilots can help ship a change in minutes, but every fast, uninspected change is a little context debt that someone else may have to pay off later. They're built to help write the next thing, not to help whoever's on call in three weeks understand what shipped today.

For a growing number of individual contributors, that shift has an uncomfortable side effect: less time spent doing the engineering they signed up for, more time spent managing an AI agent that gets the interesting part of the job and leaves them the rest.

The biggest misconception in the current conversation is that problem-solving is disappearing. It isn't—it's moved.

For decades, engineering craft lived close to the implementation layer—mastering syntax, navigating tricky code paths, hand-stitching systems together. Today, the center of gravity has shifted upward. Isolated functions or repositories don't define modern systems; they're shaped by the interactions between services, infrastructure, deployment pipelines, and now the AI-generated code running through all of it.

Here's what that looks like in practice. A product team wants to let customers undo a bulk action after it's already synced to three downstream systems—something that sounds simple until it’s actually worked through. The obvious approach is a soft-delete flag, but that breaks two other features that assume "deleted" means "gone". The right answer turns out to be an event log the system can replay backward, something none of the existing services were built around.

That's the part no AI tool gets to on its own: sitting with the shape of the problem, turning over two or three approaches, understanding why the simple one breaks and the harder one holds. Once that design is real—once the shape of what’s being built and why is clear—handing the scaffolding to an AI agent isn't a loss. It's the same relationship a senior engineer already has with a junior one: “Here's the shape, here are the constraints, go build it, and I'll review it against the design I understand.”

That moment—seeing the real shape of a hard problem before anyone writes a line to solve it—is the rush Kondov described missing: the one that used to come from sitting with a problem long enough to actually understand it. ThePrimeagen, a developer with a large following among engineers, described something similar when responding to Kondov's reflections: not the typing itself, but the thinking that used to happen before and during it, which hasn't been showing up in prompt-and-review work the way it used to.

Engineers aren't doing less meaningful work, but the joy in problem-solving has moved somewhere harder to see. And right now, most people are stuck skipping straight to the prompt instead of sitting with the problem first.

Many engineers aren't frustrated by hard problems. They're frustrated by work that stands between them and the problems they actually care about solving: the hour spent reconstructing what changed before starting debugging, the back-and-forth over who owns an issue, re-diagnosing a failure that’s already been fixed this quarter.

Most AI tooling stops at the code layer, so it doesn’t reduce overhead. Code assistants are excellent at writing and refactoring code faster, inside the file already open. But the answer to why something's breaking in production usually isn't in that file.

What's missing isn't more help writing the next thing. It's something built to make sense of what's already running. That's not a permanent condition of the job. It's a tooling problem.

Shared production context removes that overhead, opening space for higher-value work on the architecture and systems thinking that's actually interesting, not ticket triage.

When engineering craft lives at the systems layer, shared production context is what makes that craft possible at scale.

When the signals from code, telemetry, incidents, runtime behavior, and deployment history are connected in one place, engineers spend less energy jumping between tools to reconstruct basic context. PlayerZero automates away the worst parts of engineering toil—production defects, firefighting, and debugging loops—by handling the heavy lifting of signal correlation and root‑cause tracing. Engineers investigating an incident don’t have to rebuild context from scratch every time something breaks. They can spend more energy on the parts of the hunt they love: reasoning about the system and testing better solutions, even if they’re writing fewer individual lines of code by hand.

For example, at Higher Logic, support teams depended on engineering for the context needed to investigate most customer-reported issues. After adopting PlayerZero, support gained shared visibility into production behavior and the codebase. Instead of escalating, they investigate issues, validate findings, and resolve customer-facing defects before they reach engineering queues. As a result, engineering reclaimed 250 hours in two months and reduced delivery time on eligible fixes by 60%.

Instead of being pulled into every unfamiliar ticket to “take a quick look,” senior engineers had stretches of time again to make changes they trusted to hold up under real‑world conditions. The numbers show reclaimed capacity; the day‑to‑day reality was that problem-solving started to feel like the job again, not AI supervision.

Skill is quietly being redefined. Being fast with a keyboard or fluent in a language's syntax matters less than it used to. What's replacing it is the ability to mentally hold a system's behavior, to look at a strange symptom and know, or find out quickly, which of a dozen moving parts is actually responsible.

That's not a smaller kind of expertise. It's the same instinct that made debugging satisfying in the first place, tracing a problem back to its real cause, just aimed at a bigger, more interconnected target.

The engineers who enjoy that kind of work are the ones who'll find the job more engaging under this shift, not less, once they're pointed at problems that size.

What many engineers are mourning right now is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than argued away. But that feeling can make it seem like the meaningful part of the job is disappearing, when what's actually changing is where it lives.

Getting it back doesn’t require waiting for new tooling to show up in the stack. At the individual level, a few simple habits bring the thinking loop back into the job. For example, follow one incident all the way across, not just through one layer. When something breaks, don't stop once the immediate piece is fixed. Trace it upstream and downstream, what triggered it, what it touched, what would've caught it earlier. The muscle that the old debugging loop used to automatically build now has to be chosen.

Write the hypothesis before checking the logs, and guess what the dashboard will show and why. This is the fastest way to recreate the "thinking loop" AI-assisted work compresses. Being wrong and then finding out why is what made debugging satisfying in the first place.

Volunteer for the ambiguous ticket. An agent can handle scoped tickets with clear repro steps as long as a human is in the loop. The vague ticket with no clear repro—"it's slow sometimes," "customers are seeing something weird"—is where systems-level reasoning gets exercised.

Map how a feature actually behaves in production, not just how it reads in code. For an existing feature, spend twenty minutes tracing its real runtime path, what it touches, what depends on it, and what breaks if it's slow. For new ones, sketch the events, services, and edge cases first, then use AI to scaffold the code against that design. This builds the same kind of system intuition that used to come from writing every line by hand. The systems thinking and tradeoffs stay with the human, while AI handles the implementation.

Individual habits can bring an engineer’s joy back, but the right tooling makes it easier and faster at scale. What’s more difficult is making deep, systems‑level investigation the default for the entire team, even when under production pressure.

That's the harder problem AI-assisted coding hasn't solved on its own. It's also the subject of our companion piece, AI-Assisted Coding Is Great. It's Just Solving the Wrong Problem.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

#9743. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9742. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9741. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9740. CodeRabbit and Greptile Alternatives – How to Test PRs Beyond the Code Review

Release faster with AI testing that 10x your QA

Release faster with AI testing that 10x your QA

Release faster with AI testing that 10x your QA

If you’re looking for a CodeRabbit or Greptile alternative because PRs still ship bugs after a review bot has approved them, adding another reviewer is rarely the fix. What would help in this situation is running the change in a working app and checking what users actually see. That could mean reviewers with execution built in, tests your coding agent writes into your repo, or independent testing of the PR's preview deployment.

Your coding agent can open a PR in minutes, but checking that the change works for a user is still the slow part. This guide groups the alternatives by what each one verifies, gives each a fair "best for" assessment, and shows how to run a reviewer and a verifier on the same PR.

CodeRabbit reviews the diff with a large language model and runs linters and security scanners in a sandbox. It can also fix failing continuous integration (CI) checks and generate unit tests on request.

Greptile indexes your whole repository, so it can spot a change that breaks a caller three folders away. With TREX turned on, it starts your app in a sandbox built from an environment you configure, clicks through the affected flows, and posts what broke.

Both are worth having. Faros reports that many companies now run an AI review on 50% to 80% of their PRs, and heavy users see faster first reviews and lower change failure rates (a correlation, Faros notes). 👍

What a reviewer still can’t spot, though, is how the product runs in your real infrastructure. Take a PR that adds a health badge to a CRM. The badge works on the pipeline board and the deals list but is missing from the deal's own page. You only catch that when those screens load in a browser.

QA.tech documents this exact case in its demo CRM.

AI coding agents can write solid code and plenty of unit tests. But, the real question is whether the running app still works for a user. The agent that wrote a change is a poor judge of that. When it misreads the ticket, it writes a test that reflects what’s been misread. Both the code and the test pass, but the feature still doesn’t do what was asked of it.

METR found evidence of this in practice. Maintainers reviewed AI-generated pull requests that had already passed a benchmark's automated tests, but roughly half wouldn’t have been merged.

Teams are also feeling the impact of this growing volume. In Faros' Q3 2026 data, time spent on quality assurance (QA) is up 300.6%, while PRs merged with no review at all rose by 76.3%.

Finally, AI makes an existing issue worse. Scripted regression suites frequently broke when UI changes affected existing tests, long before coding agents arrived. A Microsoft Research paper found that only about 15% of review comments pointed to a possible defect. QA.tech covers the full model in its guide to the four layers of verifying coding agent work.

Here are the main alternatives to CodeRabbit and Greptile, grouped by how they review and test code.

GitHub Copilot code review, Cursor Bugbot, Qodo Merge, Graphite

Fewer comments or a better fit with your editor and PR workflow.

Same as CodeRabbit: it reads code but doesn’t run the app.

TREX runs your branch in a sandbox it builds. Vercel provides its own suggested patches against your build and tests.

Teams that want one vendor for review alongside a runtime signal.

A sandbox is not the same as your deployed preview. The reviewer picks flows unless you pin them.

Momentic, browser tools such as ChromeDevTools MCP

Whatever your coding agent chooses to test.

A tight feedback loop while the agent builds.

The same agent writes the code and the test. Your team still needs to maintain the suite.

The deployed preview checked by a system that didn’t write the change.

Teams with a high release cadence and many agent PRs.

Needs a preview environment or staging and adds a second check to the PR.

For more comprehensive comparisons, see QA.tech's roundups of CodeRabbit alternatives, Greptile alternatives, and QA tools for coding agents.

TREX builds its sandbox from a setup script that installs dependencies, runs migrations, and seeds data. Your environment variables are available only during that build, not while TREX runs its tests. Outbound network access can also be restricted.

That works for a lot of logic, but it’s weaker for flows that depend on things outside the repo, such as your real auth provider, your payment provider's test mode, feature flags served from your backend, or the email your onboarding flow sends.

For instance, take a redesigned onboarding flow that sends a verification email. In a sandbox, that email may never leave the machine. On a preview deployment, a QA agent can sign up, open the inbox, click the link, and confirm the account. ✨

Independence is another difference. With TREX, the product that reviews your diff also chooses and runs the flows, unless you pin them yourself. An independent verifier works from the ticket and user journeys.

Keep your reviewer on the diff. It catches committed API keys, risky patterns, and style issues at low cost.

Get a preview environment on every PR. If that’s not possible yet, test staging right after the merge and post the result on the merged PR. QA.tech's PR testing docs support both approaches.

Pin a small critical-path regression set. Sign-up, checkout, and payment run on every PR and block the merge. Use exploratory testing and dynamic tests based on the diff for the rest rather than rebuilding your entire existing suite.

Define compliance-critical flows as explicit steps so journeys that must never drift are easy to spot when they fail, with full traces that help you investigate the matter.

Write acceptance criteria into the ticket or PR description since the verifier reads that context.

Make the verifier's check in branch protection a requirement, and keep the merge decision with a person who now has evidence in front of them.

QA agents take over the repetitive verification, while people remain in charge of the judgment, risk calls, and usability. For guidance on what belongs on the gate, see QA.tech's PR checklist and risk-based testing for pull requests.

A reviewer plus solid unit and integration tests are enough when:

There’s no user interface, as with libraries, software development kits (SDKs), and command-line tools.

You have no preview environments and don’t plan on adding them anytime soon. Greptile with TREX can give you some runtime feedback without these.

PR volume is low enough for a person to click through every change.

⚠️ Once agent PRs outnumber the people who can review them, the manual check is the first thing teams tend to skip.

QA.tech is an AI testing platform that runs PR testing against each pull request's preview deployment. Its QA agents open the deployed app in a browser and work toward a user goal relying on what they can see on the screen, much like a real person would. That way, tests adapt when the UI changes. CodeRabbit and Greptile read the code, but this tool checks the product itself. That’s different from "self-healing," which usually means a broken locator got re-guessed (and here’s why that idea could be misleading).

On each PR, the agent reads the description, the linked Jira or Linear ticket, and the diff. It selects the existing tests that cover the change, writes new ones only where coverage is missing, and adjusts depth based on how many user flows the change can affect. The verdict is “pass,” “fail,” or "unable to verify." The last of the three means the tests never exercised your change, so you don’t get a false green. Failures come with the agent's step-by-step reasoning, screenshots, video, network activity, and console output.

QA.tech’s review of a pull request: a medium-risk change across three CRM surfaces, eight tests run, one failure showing the deal page missing its health badge.

A single test can cover the same user journey across web, native mobile, API, email and SMS, and voice. Before a PR exists, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server lets Cursor, Claude Code or Codex start runs, read results, and open a tunnel so QA agents can test your localhost. It also integrates with Jira, Linear, Slack, GitHub, and GitLab, plus a custom API for other CI systems.

For a real-world example, see the case study on replacing 320 hours of manual testing with QA agents.

PR testing is included in the free trial, so you can connect a repo and get a review on your next pull request before talking to anyone. You can start now at https://app.qa.tech/auth/sign-up.

If your team ships more agent PRs than anyone can possibly click through, the PR testing overview explains how the setup works. (Your reviewer keeps its own comment thread, so the two don’t argue. ¯\(ツ)/¯)

It depends on what your complaint is. Copilot code review or Cursor Bugbot are a good choice for less noise, Greptile for cross-file context, and PR testing for bugs that only show up when the app runs.

With TREX enabled, Greptile runs your branch in a sandbox built from your setup script, not in your deployed preview.

No. CodeRabbit runs linters and analysis tools and can generate unit tests, but it doesn’t open your running app during a review.

Yes. The reviewer covers the diff, while the verifier checks the deployed preview. Each posts its own result on the same PR.

It can for quick feedback while it builds, but the final verdict should come from a system that didn’t write the change.

#9739. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9738. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9736. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

#9735. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9734. Measuring Sales Forecast Bias With Tracking Signals and SQL

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every sales leader has a rep who sandbags and a rep with happy ears. The sandbagger commits $80,000 and books $95,000. The optimist commits $120,000 and books $100,000. Everyone in the forecast call knows who's who, and everyone adjusts in their head.

Adjusting in your head doesn't scale, and it's often wrong. People remember the dramatic misses and forget the quiet ones. Demand planners had this problem decades ago with product forecasts, and they solved it with a number called the tracking signal. It's one line of arithmetic, it runs in SQL, and it tells you whether a forecaster's misses lean one way.

A forecast can be wrong in two ways. It can be noisy: sometimes high, sometimes low, averaging out. Or it can be biased: consistently on one side.

Noise is the cost of selling. Deals slip, budgets move, a champion leaves. Nobody can forecast that away. Bias is different. It's a habit, and habits can be corrected. If a rep's commits run 15% low every month, you can either coach the habit or scale their number by 1.15 and get a better forecast for free.

The trouble is that a single month tells you nothing. A rep who over-called last month might just have lost a deal. You need to look at a run of months and ask whether the errors cancel out or pile up.

The tracking signal is the sum of the forecast errors divided by the mean absolute error, over the same window.

If the misses cancel out, the sum is close to zero and so is the signal. If every miss is in the same direction, the sum equals the number of months times the average miss, and the signal equals the number of months in the window. With a 12-month window, it runs from -12 to +12. A rep who over-calls every single month scores +12. A rep who under-calls every month scores -12.

Dividing by the mean absolute error is what makes it comparable across reps. A rep with big deals and big misses isn't penalized just for having big numbers.

I simulated two years of monthly commits for four reps. Ana calls it straight. Ben commits about 15% under what he books. Cara commits about 15% over. Dev calls it straight for a year, then starts over-calling by 25% in month 13. Every commit also has random noise of about 12%, because real forecasts do.

Here's the signal for each rep at the end of each quarter in year two:

Ben sits at -12: every miss in two years was on the low side. Cara is close to the top. Dev looks fine for the first year, then climbs steadily once the new habit kicks in. Ana wanders, which is what an honest forecaster's signal does. She touched 5.1 at one point by chance.

The commit_ratio column says how big the bias is. At month 24, Ben's commits are 0.85 of what he books and Cara's are 1.16. That's the correction factor, if you decide to use one.

Textbooks often quote ±4 as the limit. That limit was set for a different setup, and it doesn't transfer. With 12 noisy monthly forecasts, an honest rep crosses 4 all the time. I simulated it:

At ±4, you'd flag an honest rep in 39% of windows. At ±8, that drops to 7%, while still catching a 15% sandbagger almost every time and a 10% optimist about two-thirds of the time. For monthly data over a year, ±8 is a sensible starting point. Run the same simulation with your own noise level to set your own limit, because it depends on how lumpy your deals are.

Dev shows the cost of a long window. The habit started in month 13, and the signal didn't cross 8 until month 20. A shorter window reacts faster but cries wolf more often. That's a real trade-off, not a flaw in the method.

Show it in the forecast call, next to the commit. "Cara commits $140,000, tracking signal +11" is a different conversation from "Cara commits $140,000." It's also fairer than reputation, because it's measured, not remembered.

Coach first, correct second. A strong signal is a reason to ask what's going on. Sandbaggers are often protecting themselves from a comp plan or a manager who punishes misses. Optimists often haven't been asked hard questions about their deals. Fix the cause and the bias goes away.

If you correct, correct with the ratio. Multiply a rep's commit by their actual-to-commit ratio over the same window. Do it in the roll-up, openly, and tell the rep. Silent adjustments make reps game the adjustment.

Run it on the leaders too. Front-line managers and the VP forecast every week. Their bias matters more than any one rep's, because it's in the number the board sees.

The tracking signal doesn't care why someone is wrong. It just asks whether their mistakes cancel out. That's the right question for a forecast, and it's one most sales teams never measure. Supply chain planners run it on thousands of products every week. Running it on eight reps once a month is easy.

Your Win Rate Is Wrong Because of the Denominator
