#9706. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9705. Can your coding agent beat a 94% Rust speedup? 4 Wasmtime benchmarks and 11 Lean 4 math problems are still unbeaten

Most AI coding benchmarks rely on static suites or LLM-as-a-judge. I wanted to see what happens when developers point their idle coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or local CLI/MCP agents) at live, objectively verifiable challenges where every accepted pull request lands straight on main.

So I built Swarmdesk (completely free to use).

8 Rust functions compiled to WebAssembly and measured deterministically by Wasmtime instruction count ("fuel") on randomized inputs, not noisy wall-clock timing.

11 open mathematical conjectures, quantitative bounds, and composable blueprint helper lemmas.

Generate your personal desk key and either:

Humans post optimization ideas, vote, and propose new math problems, but nothing user-typed ever reaches an agent. Maintainers distill approved ideas into a single-line ASCII technical hint, and submitted Rust/Lean files cannot contain comments or string literals.

I would love honest feedback on the setup flow or anything that breaks when you try it!

#9704. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

#9701. Writing a Dockerfile: five instructions, explained one by one

To run your Python app with Docker, you first need a Dockerfile. It is the recipe for your image: a text file, named Dockerfile, that lists the steps to build it.

We made a 28-second video that goes through the five instructions you need:

You can also watch it on our site: Writing a Dockerfile.

The rest of this post goes through each instruction of the video, with the code.

A folder with two files: the code and the list of its dependencies.

Here is the file from the video. It goes at the root of the folder:

Five instructions, read from top to bottom.

An image almost always starts from an existing one. Here, Ubuntu 22.04, pulled from Docker Hub. It contains a minimal Ubuntu system and nothing else: no Python, no code of yours.

The part after the colon is the tag, which is the version. Always write one. Without it, Docker takes latest, and your build may change the day a new version comes out.

The instructions that follow (COPY, RUN, CMD) work from /app, inside the image. If the folder does not exist, Docker creates it. It is the cd of the Dockerfile, and it stays in effect when the container starts.

Two paths: the first one is on your machine, the second one is in the image. The first dot is the build context, the folder you give to docker build. The second one is the working folder, so /app. After this line, app.py and requirements.txt are in the image, along with everything else in the folder.

RUN executes a command while the image is being built, and keeps the result in the image. Here it installs Python, which the Ubuntu image does not have, then the packages listed in requirements.txt.

The -y matters: nobody is there to answer "yes" during a build.

CMD does nothing during the build. It records the default command, the one that runs when a container starts from the image. You can replace it for one run by adding a command after the image name: docker run my-app python3 other.py.

The form with brackets starts the program directly, without a shell in between, so it receives the stop signal when you stop the container.

An image is not one block. Each instruction adds a step on top of the previous ones, and Docker keeps the result of each step in its build cache. You can see them, once the image is built:

To be precise, the instructions that change files (COPY, RUN) add a layer of files, and that is where the size of the image comes from. CMD only records a setting: it shows up in the history with a size of 0B.

This is why the order of the lines matters. When you build again, Docker reuses the cache until it reaches a line that changed, or a COPY whose files changed. From that line on, everything is rebuilt.

In the file above, COPY . . comes before RUN. Change one character in app.py and Docker installs Python and all the packages again.

The file above is the simplest one to read, not the one to ship. Once the five instructions are clear, two changes make the image faster to build and much lighter:

COPY . . takes everything in the folder, including a .env file with your passwords if there is one. Add a .dockerignore file next to the Dockerfile to leave out what has no place in the image:

There is more to a production image, starting with not running the app as root. That is for another post.

The Dockerfile is only the recipe. Building the image and running a container takes two commands:

That is part 2 of the series: Building and running a container.

#9700. Beyond the Pilot: Making AI Deliver Real Business Value

Senior Architect with 16+ years in cloud, AI, trading systems.

Senior Architect with 16+ years in cloud, AI, trading systems.

Senior Architect with 16+ years in cloud, AI, trading systems.

For the last two years, every boardroom conversation has sounded the same: What’s our AI strategy?

I’ve sat in those meetings. I’ve watched leadership teams proudly showcase chatbot demos, predictive dashboards, and “AI-powered” workflows during quarterly reviews. I’ve also watched many of those same projects quietly disappear six months later—stuck in endless proof-of-concept mode, disconnected from operations, or producing results nobody trusted enough to use.

That’s the uncomfortable reality of enterprise AI right now.

Most companies are no longer asking whether AI matters. They already know it does. The real challenge is figuring out how to move beyond experimentation and make AI generate measurable business value consistently, responsibly, and at scale.

And from what I’ve seen working with IT leaders, operations teams, and digital transformation initiatives, the gap between “AI excitement” and “AI impact” usually comes down to one thing:

The organizations winning with AI today are not necessarily the ones with the biggest budgets or the flashiest demos. They are the ones treating AI like an operational capability instead of a side experiment.

The modern enterprise is full of AI pilots.

A customer support assistant gets tested in one region. A predictive maintenance model runs inside one factory. HR experiments with AI-generated job descriptions. Finance automates invoice classification for a small business unit.

At first, these projects look successful. Productivity improves. Teams get excited. Leadership announces innovation milestones.

Scaling becomes harder than expected because the underlying systems were never designed for AI-driven operations. Data is inconsistent. Security teams push back. Governance policies are unclear. Employees stop trusting outputs after a few bad recommendations. Suddenly, the “transformational” initiative becomes another isolated tool nobody fully adopts.

I’ve seen enterprises with dozens of AI pilots and almost no enterprise-wide value creation.

The problem isn’t ambition. It’s architecture.

AI doesn’t magically fix operational complexity. In many cases, it exposes how fragmented organizations already are.

Despite the hype cycles, AI is producing real business outcomes today. But the most successful use cases are surprisingly practical.

They aren’t futuristic humanoid robots replacing entire departments overnight.

They are focused, operational improvements tied directly to measurable business metrics.

The strongest AI implementations usually start with repetitive workflows.

IT service management is a good example. AI-driven ticket classification, incident summarization, and knowledge retrieval are reducing response times dramatically. Teams spend less time routing requests manually and more time solving complex issues.

The same pattern exists across finance, HR, procurement, and customer operations.

None of these use cases sound revolutionary individually. But collectively, they create something far more important: operational efficiency at scale.

One trend I didn’t fully appreciate until recently is how AI is shifting from automation into decision augmentation. This is where the technology becomes genuinely transformative. Instead of simply executing tasks faster, AI helps organizations make better decisions under uncertainty.

Retail companies are using AI models to optimize inventory forecasting. Healthcare systems are prioritizing patient interventions using predictive risk analysis. Logistics organizations are rerouting supply chains dynamically based on disruptions, weather conditions, and demand signals.

The important distinction here is subtle but critical:

It’s improving the quality and speed of decisions humans make.

That distinction matters because the most effective organizations are designing collaborative systems where human expertise and machine intelligence complement each other.

One of the clearest indicators that AI is moving beyond experimentation is how deeply it’s embedding itself into customer experience operations. Customers increasingly expect personalization, instant responses, and contextual interactions as baseline capabilities. AI-powered recommendation engines, conversational support systems, and intent analysis tools are now central to digital engagement strategies.

But here’s the nuance many organizations miss:

Customers do not care whether an interaction uses AI. They care whether it feels useful, fast, and accurate. I’ve seen companies overinvest in “human-like AI experiences” while ignoring fundamental workflow issues causing customer frustration. Meanwhile, competitors using simpler automation strategically achieve far better outcomes.

AI succeeds when it improves experiences invisibly.

Every successful AI initiative eventually runs into the same wall: data quality.

This remains the single biggest blocker to enterprise-scale AI adoption.

Organizations often underestimate how fragmented their data ecosystems really are until AI systems begin depending on them. Different departments maintain inconsistent definitions. Legacy systems store incomplete records. Critical information exists inside PDFs, emails, spreadsheets, and disconnected applications.

AI magnifies these inconsistencies quickly. A chatbot trained on outdated policies becomes unreliable. Predictive models fail because operational data lacks standardization. Recommendation systems generate irrelevant outputs because customer profiles are incomplete. This is why mature organizations are investing heavily in data governance before aggressively scaling AI initiatives.

The reality is that AI maturity is increasingly inseparable from data maturity.

Companies that spent years modernizing cloud infrastructure, standardizing data pipelines, and building governance frameworks are now moving faster than competitors trying to “bolt AI on” afterward.

There’s another challenge IT leaders rarely discuss publicly: most enterprise infrastructure still isn’t designed for AI workloads.

Many organizations operate hybrid environments stitched together over decades. Critical business logic lives inside aging ERP systems. Data moves through brittle integrations. Security policies vary across environments.

Introducing AI into that ecosystem creates enormous complexity.

And unlike traditional software deployments, AI systems evolve continuously. Models drift. Data changes. Outputs require validation.

That’s why infrastructure modernization is becoming tightly linked to AI strategy. Cloud-native architectures, unified data platforms, and scalable integration frameworks are no longer “future improvements.” They are prerequisites for sustainable AI deployment.

Another issue surfacing everywhere is the AI talent shortage. And contrary to popular belief, the biggest shortage isn’t necessarily data scientists. It’s people who understand both business operations and AI implementation realities.

Technical teams often build models without understanding operational workflows. Business leaders push AI initiatives without understanding technical limitations. The organizations making real progress are building cross-functional AI teams where IT, operations, compliance, and business stakeholders collaborate continuously.

That operational integration matters more than pure technical sophistication.

In fact, some of the most successful AI programs I’ve seen rely less on cutting-edge algorithms and more on disciplined change management, employee training, and process redesign. Because AI transformation is ultimately organizational transformation.

Early AI experimentation allowed organizations to move fast with limited oversight.

As AI systems become embedded into customer interactions, hiring workflows, financial operations, and decision-making processes, governance is becoming a board-level concern.

The speed of AI adoption has outpaced governance maturity in many organizations. Teams rushed into implementation before defining accountability structures or risk management frameworks. The smartest IT leaders I know are approaching governance not as a restriction, but as an enabler of scale.

Because responsible AI creates confidence, and confidence enables adoption.

Without governance, every AI deployment becomes a political battle between innovation teams, legal departments, compliance officers, and executives.

With governance, organizations can move faster because the rules are already defined.

After watching countless AI initiatives succeed or fail, a few patterns stand out consistently.

The organizations creating real value are focusing on five priorities.

Successful AI programs begin with operational pain points tied to measurable outcomes.

Not executive pressure to “do something with AI.”

AI systems are only as reliable as the data feeding them.

Modernizing data architecture, governance, and interoperability may feel slower than launching flashy pilots, but it creates long-term scalability.

The most effective AI systems support employees instead of attempting to replace them immediately.

Trust grows when AI improves human performance consistently.

Governance frameworks should evolve alongside deployment strategies—not after problems emerge.

Responsible AI is rapidly becoming a competitive differentiator.

Too many organizations optimize for innovation theater instead of operational integration.

Real value appears when AI becomes embedded into daily workflows, metrics, and business processes.

That requires discipline, not just experimentation.

We are entering a more mature phase of enterprise AI adoption.

The conversation is shifting away from speculative disruption and toward operational accountability.

That pressure is forcing organizations to confront an important truth:

AI success is not determined by how advanced the models are. It’s determined by how effectively organizations integrate technology, data, governance, infrastructure, and people into a coherent operating strategy. The companies that understand this are already moving beyond pilots.

And over the next few years, that difference will define who actually captures business value from AI—and who gets left behind in permanent experimentation mode.

Why Modern Data Centers Must Be Redesigned for AI-First Workloads

#9695. ASO audit with Claude: a free skill and MCP server

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at storelift.net

To run an ASO audit with Claude, install the free aso-audit skill (one SKILL.md file) and ask Claude to audit your app. With Storelift's MCP server connected, the audit reads measured keyword ranks, the apps above you, rank history, your store page, reviews and charts, and reports each check per storefront as PASS, FIX or UNKNOWN. Without the server it runs a checklist over the public listing and marks everything that needs measurement as UNKNOWN instead of estimating it.

The skill is a set of instructions, not a program. It tells Claude which checks make up an audit, which Storelift MCP tool answers each one, and when to mark a check UNKNOWN. Every check is run per storefront — one country on one platform — because each storefront has its own ranks.

The skill uses the 8 read tools it needs from the server's 85 — list_apps first, then the seven above. Every tool it names is published by the server, and an audit leaves your account exactly as it found it.

The skill is a single file: download SKILL.md. It starts with the YAML frontmatter every Agent Skill carries — a name (aso-audit) and a description that tells Claude when to use it — followed by the instructions. Read it before you install it; it is plain text.

Claude Code loads personal skills from ~/.claude/skills//SKILL.md, available in every project:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/aso-audit curl -fsSL https://storelift.net/data/aso-audit-skill/SKILL.md -o ~/.claude/skills/aso-audit/SKILL.md

To share it with a team through the repository, put it under the project's .claude/skills/ instead:

mkdir -p .claude/skills/aso-audit curl -fsSL https://storelift.net/data/aso-audit-skill/SKILL.md -o .claude/skills/aso-audit/SKILL.md

Claude picks the skill up when a request matches its description, such as “run an ASO audit of my app”. You can also call it by name with /aso-audit.

The Claude apps take custom skills as a ZIP file of the skill folder. Put SKILL.md in a folder named aso-audit, zip the folder, and upload it from the Skills area of the app's settings. Menu names change between app versions; the file stays the same.

The measured mode needs the Storelift MCP server in the same client. In Claude Code, add the hosted endpoint and sign in with /mcp:

claude mcp add --transport http storelift https://storelift.net/mcp

Claude Desktop setup, the npm package and the Claude.ai connector are on the MCP server guide. The hosted server works through sign-in on Pro and above; the checklist mode runs on the public listing alone.

The first four use measured data and need the MCP server. The last two work in either mode; in checklist mode, paste your keyword field into the chat — it lives in your App Store Connect account.

One report per storefront. It opens with the mode (measured, with the measurement time, or checklist) and a count of checks: how many passed, how many need fixing, how many are UNKNOWN.

The report keeps counts per check instead of one blended score, so every check that needs work stays visible by name, with the evidence behind it.

Without the MCP server, the skill points each UNKNOWN to a free tool that answers it one term at a time: rank check, keyword difficulty, the keyword field packer and the character counter.

When a number is missing, the report says UNKNOWN and names the data that would fill it, so every number printed in the report is a measured one.

Q: Is the ASO audit skill free? A: Yes. The SKILL.md file is free to download and use. The checklist mode needs nothing else. The measured mode uses Storelift's MCP server, which starts on Pro.

Q: Does it work in Claude Code? A: Yes. Save it as ~/.claude/skills/aso-audit/SKILL.md for all projects, or under the project's .claude/skills/. Claude uses it when you ask for an ASO audit, or you can run /aso-audit.

Q: Does it give my app an ASO score? A: It reports, per storefront, how many checks passed, need fixing or are UNKNOWN. Counts keep every check that needs work visible by name.

Q: Can it audit a competitor's app? A: In checklist mode it reviews any public listing you point it to. The measured tools read the apps tracked in your Storelift account, and rivals appear there as the apps ranking above you, with their ranks and rating counts.

Q: Does it change my App Store listing? A: The skill writes a report, and what you ship stays your decision. To act on it from the chat, the MCP server's update_listing tool (Studio) writes listing text to an editable App Store version after a preview and your confirmation; the text waits in the draft until you submit it.

#9692. Chocolate-Covered Strawberry Turkeys

Turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can also be the star of dessert if you stretch your imagination enough. This idea first gained popularity on TikTok, using chocolate-dipped strawberries, marshmallows, pretzel rods, and melted chocolate to create these adorable little treats.

#9689. Why Are We Still So Easy to Fool in the Age of Unlimited Information?

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

We gave the world access to knowledge. We also gave every bad explanation a publishing platform, an audience, and somewhere to belong.

Some time ago, while working on my research into why people believe in pseudoscience and anti-scientific claims, I kept coming back to a question: why do people hold on to explanations supported by so little evidence? I had been looking at astrology, numerology, homeopathy, vaccine myths, and conspiracy theories—not because they are identical, but because each reveals something about what we want an explanation to do for us.

After finishing that piece, another question bothered me more.

We now carry what would once have looked like an absurdly powerful research library in our pockets. A claim about medicine can be checked against clinical evidence. A claim about the stars can be compared with astronomy. An elaborate conspiracy can, at least in principle, be examined against documents, dates, and independent accounts. So why haven't these beliefs simply faded away?

Part of the answer is that we handed the library keys to everyone. Including the people selling the nonsense.

The internet did not merely give us access to reliable knowledge. It gave almost anyone the ability to publish a competing version of reality, discover a receptive audience, and build a community around it. An unsupported claim no longer has to survive in isolation. It can acquire a website, a podcast, a thousand videos, an app, and a group of people ready to explain why the critics are wrong.

My argument is not that technology made humanity uniquely irrational. It is that we expected a problem of human judgment to disappear when we solved a problem of information delivery. Those were never the same problem.

There was a reasonable optimism behind the early promise of the web. Knowledge would no longer be trapped behind a university wall, an expensive encyclopedia, or the accident of where someone was born. A teenager could learn astrophysics. A worried parent could read medical guidance. Someone suspicious of a grand historical claim could compare competing accounts without waiting for an expert to visit the town library.

Those gains are real. Yet the optimistic version quietly assumed that making the good explanation available would make the bad explanation less attractive. Information was treated rather like clean water: improve the supply, and people will naturally drink it.

But information is not water. A person does not always prefer the most carefully supported explanation. Sometimes we prefer the explanation that removes a frightening uncertainty. Sometimes we want a villain, a cosmic plan, or the satisfaction of being among the few who have "figured it out." And sometimes we simply trust the person sharing the story more than we trust the institution disputing it.

These motives matter in different ways. A tarot reading can be a harmless ritual of reflection. A claim that a homeopathic remedy can replace proven treatment is a medical claim with consequences. A conspiracy theory can offer an enemy and a ready-made community. A vaccine rumor may grow from a genuine fear, then become an identity marker. They are not interchangeable, and the consequences certainly are not. What they share is that the factual strength of an explanation is only one of the things people may value about it.

The psychologist Karen Douglas and colleagues have described the appeal of conspiracy theories through several kinds of motives: the wish to understand events, the wish for security and control, and the wish to protect a social identity. That is not a universal diagnosis for every believer, but it helps explain why another fact sheet may miss the point. A fact sheet answers a question about evidence. The person may also be asking whether the world is safe, whether their community can be trusted, or whether they still matter in it.

The internet is exceptionally good at serving the second set of questions. It may offer not just an answer, but other people who find that answer comforting.

An unusual belief once depended heavily on local surroundings: family conversations, a bookshop shelf, a television show, perhaps a small organization that printed newsletters. People still encounter ideas that way. But a believer in a far-fetched explanation can now find a community across the planet in minutes. That can be socially meaningful long before it becomes intellectually convincing.

Picture a hypothetical person unsettled by a medical decision. They type a worried question into a search box. One result leads to a personal testimony. The testimony links to a forum. The forum offers a video. The video introduces a creator who appears knowledgeable, patient, and sympathetic. The person returns the next day because the community has noticed their concerns. A week later, the issue is not just whether an assertion is true. It is also whether the people who welcomed them are wrong.

This is an illustration, not a claim that every worried patient follows this path or that every platform sends users down it. But it captures an important distinction: the network can turn a claim into a relationship.

Websites supply an archive. Search makes it discoverable. Social feeds give it repeated exposure. Private chats let people circulate it without public scrutiny. Applications make the practice routine; a daily horoscope or a numerology notification can become part of a morning ritual. Online groups provide shared language, jokes, heroes, enemies, and a sense of belonging. No single technology does all of this. Together, they can give a belief a surprisingly durable home.

It is tempting to imagine that each new follower has been convinced by an argument. Often the process can be more ordinary. An idea appears frequently, then begins to look familiar; people around us repeat it, then it begins to look respectable. A 2026 meta-analysis covering 182 studies found that repetition can increase perceived truth on average, although effects vary substantially by context and type of statement. Familiarity is not proof, but it has a way of borrowing proof's clothing.

One of the internet's peculiar achievements is that a claim can arrive at our screen already surrounded by social evidence: comments, reactions, creators, testimonials, and apparent consensus. None of those features establishes whether the claim is correct. Yet they change how the encounter feels. The old village rumor has learned how to count its followers.

The phrase filter bubble suggests an invisible machine that surrounds us with acceptable ideas. The phrase echo chamber suggests a room where our own opinions return to us louder. Both are useful metaphors. Both are also capable of misleading us if we mistake the metaphor for a complete explanation.

There are at least three processes worth separating.

First, we choose. We search with particular words, follow particular people, leave annoying groups, and return to places where we feel understood. Someone who searches for "why this treatment is dangerous" is starting from a different question than someone who searches for "what do clinical trials say about this treatment?" The results may reflect that difference even before a recommendation algorithm gets involved.

Second, our communities choose with us. Friends recommend sources. Group administrators set norms. People who challenge the shared story may lose standing or simply stop participating. A community does not need to ban disagreement formally to make disagreement expensive. Social belonging can do much of the work.

Third, platforms select and rank. Search engines and feeds cannot show everything at once. They decide what is visible, what appears early, what is recommended next, and what never gets encountered at all. Ranking is unavoidable at scale; the meaningful questions are which signals it uses, what it optimizes, and how it interacts with human preferences.

Research has documented echo-chamber patterns. A 2021 PNAS study compared more than 100 million pieces of content across several social platforms and found different patterns of like-minded connections and information sharing. That is evidence of selective clustering, not proof that a single algorithm mechanically creates every extreme belief.

Here is where the evidence becomes more interesting than the standard internet horror story. In a 2023 field experiment involving 23,377 Facebook users during the 2020 US election, researchers reduced exposure to posts from like-minded sources by about one-third. They did not find corresponding measurable reductions in political polarization over the study period. Related experiments changing chronological versus algorithmic feeds also changed what people encountered without significantly changing several measured political attitudes over three months.

These were studies of particular political settings, not direct tests of astrology, homeopathy, or every conspiracy community. They do not absolve platforms of influence. They do tell us not to present the bubble as a switch that an engineer could simply turn off. Beliefs have histories, relationships, habits, and identities attached to them. Changing a feed is not the same as changing a mind.

I find that both more reassuring and more disturbing. Reassuring, because people are not programmable puppets. Disturbing, because our own choices can maintain the room even when the door is open.

The most unsettling part of this story is that the person inside a misinformation community may genuinely believe they are doing research. We often picture the problem as a refusal to look things up. Sometimes the person is looking things up constantly.

Consider a false claim that has acquired its own vocabulary. Search for it in those exact terms and you may find websites built to repeat it, articles quoting one another, and videos citing the same weak source through several layers. Ten links can look like ten independent confirmations when they are actually ten roads back to a single assertion.

There is a name for the problem researchers have observed here: data voids—search areas where limited trustworthy content makes low-quality material unusually visible. It is not true of every search. But the general design risk is clear: search results reflect available pages and ranking decisions, not an automatic audit of reality.

A particularly relevant study published in Nature reported five experiments in which searching online to evaluate misleading news could increase belief in it. The researchers found evidence consistent with a role for lower-quality results. This is a narrow, experimentally studied effect, not a claim that Google or online search always makes people more credulous. Its philosophical implication is larger than its scope: the act of checking is not enough if the checking process cannot distinguish independent evidence from recycled assertion.

It is a painful irony. We may mistake effort for rigor. We spent two hours reading, so surely we know more than someone who skimmed an official summary. But hours of exposure are not the same as hours of verification. An elaborate conspiracy can demand extraordinary amounts of reading while arranging that every failure of proof becomes evidence of a deeper cover-up.

That is why conspiracy theories can appear complex yet offer a remarkably simple emotional structure: someone planned this, someone is hiding it, and someone has discovered the secret. The details multiply. The underlying story stays comfortingly stable.

Science often offers the opposite bargain. Its methods are complicated, but its conclusions may be unsatisfying: the evidence is incomplete; the causes are multiple; the result is probabilistic; the answer may change. It asks us to accept uncertainty without inventing a person responsible for it. Human beings are not always enthusiastic customers for that offer.

It would be convenient to blame the technology industry for all of this. It would also repeat the very habit this essay is criticizing: replacing a complicated reality with one villain.

Platforms have responsibilities. Product teams make choices about recommendations, moderation, sharing friction, source visibility, and how engagement is rewarded. Researchers have examined how false news diffuses online; a major 2018 Science study of fact-checked stories on Twitter between 2006 and 2017 found that false stories tended to spread farther and faster than true ones in that dataset. But those results are not a universal law of every social network in 2026. Nor do they demonstrate that all users believe everything they share.

The human side does not disappear when we demand better systems. Someone who doubts a medical institution because of a personal experience may not become trusting because the platform places a verification label on a post. Someone whose friends all belong to a conspiracy group may face a genuine social cost for leaving it. Someone who reads tarot for comfort may not even be making the factual claim a skeptic assumes they are making.

There are also limits to the idea that everyone is abandoning science. A 2025 study drawing on 71,922 respondents across 68 countries found that most people in most surveyed countries trusted scientists. There is no need to invent a universal collapse of reason to recognize the serious consequences of particular unsupported beliefs.

More information can help. Clearer explanations can help. Better platform design can help. Teaching people to recognize manipulation techniques has shown promise in controlled studies. None is a magic patch, and they operate on different parts of the problem.

I would rather ask a more uncomfortable question of both engineers and readers: what would count as evidence that our own favored explanation is wrong?

If the answer is "nothing," then the size of the library is irrelevant. We are not using it to learn. We are using it to decorate an answer we already chose.

The internet is one of humanity's great achievements. It has made obscure knowledge accessible, connected isolated people, supported independent investigation, and given ordinary individuals a voice. Those are reasons to value it, not to retreat from it.

But the same openness that lets an excellent explanation cross borders lets an unfounded one do the same. The same tools that help a scientific community collaborate can help an anti-scientific community coordinate. The same ability to find people who understand you can become a powerful reason not to listen to anyone else. This is not an accidental contradiction. It is part of what it means to build a network for humans rather than a machine for distributing certified truths.

We imagined an encyclopedia and built a public square with an encyclopedia attached. In the square, knowledge competes not only with error, but with identity, fear, entertainment, belonging, and the irresistible appeal of a good story.

I do not think the answer is to make the public square silent. I think it is to stop treating availability as understanding and popularity as evidence. The uncomfortable work is learning to ask where a claim came from, whether its sources are genuinely independent, what would disprove it, and what part of our identity we have attached to believing it.

A century from now, people may have tools that make today's search engines look primitive. They may still enjoy horoscopes. They may still find conspiracies that explain every disappointment. The technology will have changed. The desire for certainty, belonging, and a world that makes sense may not have changed nearly as much.

The question is no longer whether we can reach the truth. It is whether we are willing to recognize it when it asks us to give up a story we love.

The studies below support the factual sections; the broader argument is my own interpretation.

#9686. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9684. 25 Midwestern Thanksgiving Recipes That Bring The Nostalgia (& The Flavor)

Even nicer than Midwest nice (and that's saying something!).

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

For this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

We’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for. Plus, you can easily make it ahead and travel with it, making it an ideal potluck recipe.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. The hollowed-out potatoes are an excellent vessel for extra-creamy mashed potatoes, stuffing, turkey, and dollops of cranberry sauce.

Essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a new, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

Most sweet potato casseroles have only marshmallows or pecans. Don't even think about making this mistake. Topping with a pecan streusel and then marshmallows helps this Thanksgiving casserole stand out above all the rest.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with a wildly satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Step aside, all other casseroles—corn is not to be overlooked on the holiday table. If you prefer, drained and rinsed canned corn can be used instead of frozen, and you could substitute more milk in for the heavy cream. The finished casserole won't be quite as decadent, but it will still be delicious.

Deviled eggs are great, but when you have them for every holiday, it just makes sense to change them up sometimes. These are our new obsession

If green beans dressed up as cheesy garlic bread, then they would become these Parmesan roasted green beans. Tossed in garlic and black pepper and showered with cheese, this simply irresistible side dish will steal the spotlight at every holiday table.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for.

#9682. Ant Group Open-Sources LingSante: Why Open Medical AI Matters

Good medical AI has mostly lived behind paywalls and private APIs. Developers could use it. But they couldn't look inside it, tune it for their own patients, or run it in their own hospital. Ant Group, the tech giant behind Alipay, is changing that with LingSante, a family of open-source medical AI models built on its Ant Ling foundation model. The weights are arriving in phases, and the first two core models are already out. Open weights in healthcare AI are still unusual. So, this release deserves a close look from anyone building in the space.

LingSante is a family rather than a single model. It spans image understanding, long-context clinical reasoning, risk prediction, safety checks and live consultation. Two models lead the launch, and they are built for quite different jobs.

The family also comes with some real-world mileage. It has been tested on the Afu app, an AI health app which has 150 million users and handles 20 million consultations a day. Plenty of medical AI models are only ever shown on curated benchmarks, so traffic at that scale tells you something different.

Air-VL has 124B parameters in total, but only 5.5B are active when it runs. That sparse setup is what makes it light enough for on-device deployment, and it's aimed at personal users and smaller institutions. It takes text, images and video as input.

Flash sits at the other end. It has 560B total parameters, roughly 25B of them active, and a 1M-token context window. That context length matters for complex cases, because a real patient history is long, messy and full of details that a short window would simply cut off.

Ant Group points it at evidence-based retrieval and long-horizon clinical agents. Think of workflows where software has to plan several steps, pull in references and keep track of a case over days, not just answer one question and stop.

A model is only as trustworthy as the way it's tested, and vendors grading their own work rarely convince anyone. So Ant built InclusionMed, an open evaluation platform, together with 29 institutions including Stanford, Harvard and Peking Union Medical College. In the platform's inaugural rankings, LingSante-3.1-flash took the No.1 spot among all open-source medical models.

A ranking isn't clinical proof, and nobody should treat it like one. Still, outside institutions sharing the scoreboard is a better starting point than a company publishing its own numbers.

Three more models complete the family. Pulse predicts risk for more than 150 conditions. MedGuard handles safety, a layer that many healthcare AI projects bolt on far too late. Live is a real-time video consultation agent, and it's already running inside the Afu app.

Splitting these jobs into separate models is a useful design hint. Developers can mix and match pieces instead of betting everything on one giant system.

When the weights are public, a university lab or a small clinic-software team can study a serious medical AI model, fine-tune it for local languages and conditions, and host it on their own hardware. Closed systems rarely allow any of that, and teams with small cloud budgets usually get left out entirely.

Openness also invites scrutiny. Researchers can poke at the model, hunt for failure cases and publish what they find. In a field where errors can hurt patients, that outside pressure is a feature.

Benchmark wins and a huge user base are encouraging, but they don't replace clinical validation. Anyone building on LingSante should test it on their own patient population, keep a clinician in the loop and check local regulations before it goes near a real care decision. It's also worth remembering that the family is still rolling out, so the specialist models may take a while to reach the same level of access.

This release won't settle the debate over AI in medicine. It does hand the global health tech community something solid to work with: an on-device multimodal model, a long-context reasoning model and an open scoreboard to compare them on. It also shows what open-source medical AI can look like in practice. For developers, the practical next step is simple. Both models are available on Hugging Face and ModelScope, so you can test air-VL on your own images and flash on your longest case notes, then compare the results against whatever you use today. What people build with it over the next year will say more than any press release.
