#9562. The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

#9561. 8 Graza Olive Oil Alternatives Worth Buying

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Walk into the closest grocery store near you, ask an employee where that cool fun olive oil is, and they'll take you to a (metaphorically) glowing row of funky green squeeze bottles. These are, of course, Graza bottles. It's the sensational olive oil brand that rode to fame on the slick, green waves of cute packaging and a quality product. Graza's oil comes primarily from Jaén, Spain. The company commits to a single origin and single varietal mission, so the oil in your newly-acquired bottle comes from a single place and a single type of olive.

You'll undoubtedly notice that Graza has some acolytes waiting on the shelves next to its empire of squeeze bottles. Whether they existed before or after Graza debuted on the scene, each of these unique oils takes after Graza in some way; some are also from Andalusia, while others sport a youthful aesthetic. If you're interested in what's beyond Graza olive oil, we think these alternatives are totally worth trying out.

Hopping onto the green squeeze-bottle trend is O Olive Oil and Vinegar's organic California Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Though do note that the olive oil also comes in glass bottle form, so there's a version for everyone's packaging preferences. Olive oil-heads will enjoy the fruity notes in this oil that evoke Graza's Sizzle product. Squeeze it into a hot pan for a delicately sweet cooking oil, or combine with any of O's extensive line of vinegars in a dressing or marinade so good you'll want to drink it.

These bottles proudly wear that tantalizing "first cold pressed" label that tingles our wallets, which is the first signal that you're looking at a quality olive oil. Though all extra virgin olive oils are cold pressed and kept below 80 F, first cold pressed means that the olives were only crushed (or processed) once, making for a richer oil with more nutrients. Besides the label, O California Extra Virgin Olive Oil has a really pleasant flavor that'll be a talented supporting player in your culinary ensemble.

A Greek olive oil whose name screams professional, The Chef's Way oil by Iliada is in a squeeze bottle to provide convenient flavor whenever you need it. The Chef's Way is single-variety and pulsing with Mediterranean flavor like almonds and artichokes, which breaks up your regularly scheduled olive oil programming with a nicely acidic interlude.

It may be scary for the olive oil purists to be accosted by an aisle of squeeze bottles when you walk into the store nowadays. But one easy, squeezy afternoon of cooking will change their minds completely with the undeniable convenience. The Chef's Way olive oil comes in several different flavors, including Kalamata PDO Extra Virgin and Premium Greek Extra Virgin, so you can choose whichever variation calls to you the most. Put on your chef whites, nonslip shoes, and backwards hat, because The Chef's Way is coming to transform your home kitchen into one of those casually elegant eateries.

Costco lovers, you're going to appreciate this find. The Kirkland-branded olive oil warrants its own inclusion in this article because of its robust flavor and versatility. Like Graza, Kirkland's best olive oil comes from Spain, the country that beats Italy as the top olive oil producer in the world.

The Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil comes in an absurdly large jug, like many other items at Costco, so you'll get an incredible value for your money. It's the perfect olive oil to use in baking to add a strong, but not abrasive, creaminess. For instance, an olive oil cakes would be the perfect vehicle for the Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Olive oil cake batters tend to eat up a cup or more of oil, which can get really expensive really fast. You can save your fancy olive oil for other pursuits. But don't worry — this olive oil isn't only suited for baking. It can accommodate your shallow frying and vinaigrette needs, as well.

Another Spanish olive oil from Jaén, Oro Bailén has that slick aesthetic appeal of Graza, along with the high-quality taste. While it can be a little pricier than Graza, it offers something Graza does not: A slightly more acidic olive oil for those times when you want a punchier flavor. The brand offers a few different intensities, so you can choose how much punch you want in your olive oil. Along with the punch, you'll find notes of banana that add a ripeness you don't encounter so often with run-of-the-mill olive oils.

Oro Bailén oils comes from Picual olives, harvested very early and milled very quickly to obtain what it instead calls "olive juice," bringing to mind a flavorful and nourishing elixir you'll want to have in your kitchen. Oro Bailén has a forward quality in its flavor: outgoing, fruity, and spicy. Like Graza, which also sells potato chips, Oro Bailén has some intriguing offshoot products, like EVOO pearls and an olive oil jam for when a simple oil isn't enough to put on bread.

Featuring sleek labeling that tells you everything you need to know about the brand, Brightland Extra Virgin Olive Oil belongs to the same cool kids club that Graza is currently the ringleader of. Brightland's product line also closely resembles Graza's, offering several different types of oils for different purposes, including a popular pizza oil (which is different from olive oil). Brightland is the kind of olive oil you'll want to casually leave out on your dinner table to impress your guests.

High in polyphenols, which have healthy antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, Brightland feels as attractively carefree as it looks. The brand has also branched out into different varieties and flavors of oil, as mentioned above, in a manner more abstract and artsy than Graza. "Lucid," "Rosette," and "Arise" are some of the olive oil options when it comes to Brightland, signifying lemon, garlic, and basil. These options give you the same carefree star power you can feel when putting down a bottle of Graza on your table.

If Martha Stewart tells you to get some olive oil, you can expect two things: It'll be wicked expensive, and likely delicious. Flamingo Estate's olive oil line is perhaps a more luxurious option than Graza's, but it has a peppery bite thanks to the quick processing that will be reminiscent of Graza's "drizzle" finishing oil. Martha Stewart swears by this $50 bottle, the olives of which come from Ojai, California.

This oil is green, sumptuous, and glossy — you'll want to dip a finger into it. Though it is cosmically destined for a hunk of crusty bread, Flamingo Estate's oil also has a high smoke point, so you can use this verdant gold in the oven or on the stovetop. The look of it is one of its best qualities, so a fresh drizzle will be a beautiful finish to your dishes. It isn't unlike Martha, when you think about it: It's vibrant, tasteful, and one of the fanciest things you could come across in your kitchen.

Kosterina is an award-winning Greek olive oil, and right away you can tell: Its shiny white bottle looks like it was plucked right from the Mediterranean. The olives for this brand are harvested early, so the resulting olive oil is a little more assertive than Graza's Sizzle, but it's just as versatile. This is a single varietal olive oil, made from only Koroneiki olives that are nutrient- and oil-rich. Single varietal oils can have a crisper flavor compared to blends, and Kosterina is as refined as they come.

Buying a metal bottle of Kosterina olive oil — metal, as it helps prevent oxidation and harmful chemicals leaching into the oil from plastic — feels intentional in a similar way to getting one from Graza. It feels a little better for the environment, and it even tastes like it's doing you good. Another way that Graza's changed the home-cooking game: No longer can a home kitchen function with one singular olive oil. Now, you need one for cooking and another one for drizzling. Kosterina follows suit with this idea, offering even more choices for your olive oil-purchasing escapades.

A wildly popular olive oil, California Olive Ranch feels a little more homey than some of the other brands on this list. But it's just as good as them: The brand is is backed up by glowing reviews from both customers and publications alike. It offers its olive oil in regular pour bottles, squeeze bottles, oil sachets (for all your emergency olive oil purposes), and even spray cans for your baking pan needs. The grassy, cushiony flavor of this oil makes it one of Giada De Laurentiis' top favorite olive oil brands. In terms of an everyday, affordable olive oil that's still comparable to Graza, California Olive Ranch is where it's at.

With California Olive Ranch, you'll find some top-tier qualities you may be looking for in an olive oil: a balanced taste along with an all-purpose use. Its affordability is just the cherry on top for this great olive oil brand you should try if you want a Graza alternative.

#9557. 8 of our employee-owners’ favorite family recipes for the holidays  : Celebrate the season with us.

The holidays are always a big deal here at King Arthur, and this year we’re celebrating with something extra-special: our brand-new Enjoy the Bake campaign, which is all about the joy of baking together.

Enjoy the Bake is a reminder that memories are made around a mixing bowl, and traditions are passed down in the kitchen. In honor of this precious holiday baking season, our employee-owners are sharing the family-favorite recipes that mean the most to them this time of year.

“Every year since I was in grade school, my mom and I would spend the night before Thanksgiving making every type of pie that the family wants. We were a family of six, and everyone's taste was different. What makes it such a lasting memory is how much of a well-oiled machine my mom and I were when working together in the kitchen. She would make pie crust, and I would make all the fillings! Years later, we still make pies for the holidays — but in our own homes — and then come together for the holiday.”

Martina Fleurrey, Customer Experience Supervisor

Get the recipes: Apple Pie, Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, and Pumpkin Pie

“I grew up with my grandparents making giant batches of pizzelle for the holidays. Their delicate crunch and subtle hint of vanilla are things I'll always associate with the season. My dad now has the pizzelle press, and every holiday, we carry on the tradition, taking turns pouring the batter, pressing, and carefully removing each one.”

“My mom and I entered a gingerbread house contest every year, and making that together was so fun, as was shopping for the candy. More than once, our design was completely themed around a weird gummy shape we couldn't say no to. It was an opportunity to bake gingerbread in increasingly odd shapes, get creative with themes and ingredients, and channel our cheeky humor.” (Learn how to make your own gingerbread house in our new On-Demand Class: Gingerbread House Baking, Building & Decorating.)

Annabelle Shippee, Social Media Strategist

Get the recipe: Construction Gingerbread for Gingerbread Houses

“Each year on Thanksgiving my paternal grandmother, who had 10 kids, would make pies and bring them to each of her local kids. One year, she made two for us, as we were having a big gathering and pumpkin is my dad's favorite pie — one pie was for the gathering and one for just our family. My dad put his personal pumpkin pie upstairs in the closet. About a month later, I hear a screech and come running: My mom found the pie … which was now all moldy. We still laugh about that to this day. The last couple of years, I've been making our Pumpkin Cheesecake Pie as a new elevated version of my grandmother's classic pumpkin pie. It's been a fan favorite, and it's so beautiful to slice.”

Jordan Kilby, Director, Digital Marketing and Customer Data

“One of our family traditions is sausage bread on Christmas Eve. It's served as an appetizer (but to be honest, we all eat enough of it to be a full meal). This is one of my favorite family recipes, not only because it's delicious, but it's also nostalgic. My grandmother made it every year, and my Aunt Millie included it as one of the recipes to pass down in a family cookbook she created. My brother and I have baked it for many years, and now my kids are starting to take over the baking. (We are all still doing the eating.) It's so good that everyone looks forward to it — probably the reason it's lasted four generations.”

Get the recipe: The dough is similar to this Braided Stromboli recipe, using Italian sausage, parsley, and Romano cheese as the filling

“We started having Cranberry Orange Scones on Christmas morning back when I was a little kid. We'd use the King Arthur scone mix and the special scone pan; I loved pressing the dough into the wedge-shaped wells. At one point, we decided that we'd use orange juice as the liquid in the dough instead of milk for extra orange flavor, and that became our ‘secret trick’ that made the scones so delicious. Nowadays, we make the recipe from scratch (even though I still love the box mix) and have scones and coffee while we open stockings on Christmas morning. They're the perfect treat for our family — they feel special without being fussy, so we're able to mix them up and bake them fresh without taking away from our family time.”

“My mom has a late fall birthday, and since childhood she has insisted that instead of a cake she get a pumpkin pie to celebrate. So over the years, in the weeks between her birthday and Thanksgiving, my family ate a lot of pumpkin pie in all varieties: store-bought, homemade, topped with pecans and whipped cream, graham cracker crust and flaky pastry. When my sister's child was born, I went and stayed with her to hang out, clean laundry, and bake comfort food. When my mom showed up to visit, I had a batch of our Test Kitchen's pumpkin pie bars handy. Upon trying them she declared they were ‘the best pumpkin pie she had ever eaten.’ Since then, they have reigned pumpkin pie supreme and been the most requested dessert on the Dyer family holiday table.”

Cecile Dyer, Senior Video Producer, Baking Education

#9556. Krispy Kreme Is Bringing Rudolph To Life With A Brand-New Christmas Doughnut Collection

Who needs a glowing red nose when you've got doughnuts this festive?

If you want to bring ho-ho-home some holiday cheer, Krispy Kreme has you covered with its brand-new Rudolph Christmas Collection. Inspired by the classic 1964 Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer film, the doughnut chain is whipping up festive, sugary treats featuring some of the movie’s most beloved characters.

The newcomers are the Rudolph, Bumble, and Sam the Snowman Doughnuts. Rudolph starts with an Original Glazed doughnut dipped in icing, then gets a glittery Christmas garland sprinkle blend, vanilla-flavored frosting, and a Rudolph wreath decoration.

The Bumble Doughnut has an unglazed shell filled with raspberry filling and dipped in vanilla icing. It's finished with a vanilla frosting garland, white glitter sprinkles, and a Bumble fondant piece. Finally, the Sam the Snowman Doughnut starts with an Original Glazed dipped in vanilla icing and covered in white chocolate curls, then gets a buttercreme Christmas tree and Sam the Snowman fondant piece.

“We love giving fans new ways to enjoy the traditions they grew up with, and this collection is all about bringing people together over something fun, festive and delicious,” Alison Holder, Chief Product and Brand Officer at Krispy Kreme, said in a statement.

The new collection arrives November 28 at participating Krispy Kreme locations nationwide, just two days after the chain wraps up its Thanksgiving doughnut collection. That lineup featured four holiday-inspired flavors: Berry Cobbler, Caramel Pumpkin, Double Chocolate Crumble, and Cinnamon Apple Filled.

As for the new Rudolph treats, you can pick them up individually or grab a dozen in a special collectible-style box featuring the beloved characters.

#9555. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.
